contracts/hashing.py:R5:_normalize_froze: R5 `isinstance(obj, float)` — first arm of the recursive normalizer that runs immediately before `rfc8785.dumps()`. This is the ONLY point at which a bare Python float is inspected for finiteness on the contracts-layer hashing path, and it is Tier-1 integrity, not input validation: rfc8785 will happily emit a bare `NaN` token, producing an audit digest no verifier can re-derive and no JSON parser will read back. `isinstance` rather than `type(obj) is float` is deliberate so float subclasses reach the same rejection. Placement is also load-bearing — bool is an int, not a float, so booleans correctly skip this arm rather than being probed with math.isnan. Crash path: ValueError propagating out of `canonical_json` / `stable_hash` to whichever audit write called it, which is the intended fail-closed behaviour. Invalidated if rfc8785 grows its own non-finite rejection, or if floats are normalized upstream before reaching this module.

R5 `isinstance(obj, frozenset)` — a rejection arm, not a conversion arm, and that is the point. A frozenset has no canonical ordering, so serializing one would make the digest depend on set iteration order: the exact non-determinism `stable_hash` exists to eliminate. The arm raises TypeError rather than silently sorting because sorting is not total over mixed element types, so a "helpful" sort would itself be order-dependent for heterogeneous sets. Note the asymmetry with `_stable_repr` below, which DOES sort frozensets — that is the already-failed fallback path where determinism-within-a-version is the most that is on offer. Invalidated if a canonical frozenset encoding is defined (the tagged `entries` envelope that `core/canonical.py` uses for non-string-keyed mappings would be the natural model).

R5 `isinstance(obj, Mapping)` against the collections ABC rather than `dict`, and the choice of ABC is the whole reason this arm is correct. `deep_freeze` produces `MappingProxyType`, which is a Mapping but NOT a dict; narrowing this test to `dict` would let every frozen contract mapping skip normalization and reach rfc8785, which rejects MappingProxyType outright. The dict comprehension in the body is what converts the proxy back to a real dict. This is nominal typing against a stdlib ABC we do not own but whose membership is explicit (MappingProxyType is a registered Mapping), not structural duck-typing. Invalidated if `deep_freeze` stops emitting MappingProxyType, or if rfc8785 learns to serialize Mapping subclasses directly.

R5 `isinstance(obj, (list, tuple))` — a union arm, and the two types are grouped rather than split because their normalization is genuinely identical: both become a JSON array. `tuple` is in the union for the same reason MappingProxyType is covered above — it is what `deep_freeze` produces for sequences, and rfc8785 accepts only `list`. Contrast the checkpoint serializer, where tuple gets its OWN envelope because that path needs round-trip fidelity; here the output is a hash input, so tuple-ness is not semantic and collapsing it is correct. Invalidated the moment a caller needs `(1, 2)` and `[1, 2]` to hash differently.
contracts/hashing.py:R5:_stable_repr:ast: R5 `isinstance(obj, dict)` opening `_stable_repr`, the `repr_hash` fallback used only after `canonical_json` has already failed — i.e. on data that is known malformed and being quarantined. The arm sorts by `repr(key)` rather than by key, and that is why the check is here: on this path keys may be of mixed, mutually non-comparable types, so a plain `sorted(obj.items())` would raise TypeError and turn a quarantine into a crash. `isinstance` rather than an exact type check so dict subclasses (Counter, defaultdict, OrderedDict) also get deterministic ordering instead of falling through to their own repr. Invalidated if `repr_hash` ever acquires a cross-version stability requirement — repr-based hashing cannot meet it, and the fix would be a real encoding, not a change to this test.

R5 `isinstance(obj, frozenset)` in the ternary `prefix = "frozenset" if ... else ""`, nested inside the `(set, frozenset)` arm above. This second, narrower check is what stops `{1, 2}` and `frozenset({1, 2})` from producing byte-identical reprs and therefore identical `repr_hash` digests — two distinct values colliding in the quarantine audit record. It is a value-distinguishing check, not a type-dispatch check: both branches take the same code path and differ only in the literal prefix, which is why the ternary form is right and a separate elif arm would be worse. Invalidated only by a policy decision that set and frozenset are hash-equivalent for quarantined data.

R5 `isinstance(obj, (set, frozenset))` — grouped as a union because the treatment that matters here (sort the element reprs so iteration order cannot leak into the digest) is identical for both. They are deliberately NOT distinguished at this level; the one place they must differ is the repr prefix chosen one line below. Splitting this into two arms would duplicate the sorting logic for no semantic gain. Invalidated if set and frozenset acquire different element-ordering rules.

R5 `isinstance(obj, tuple)` nested inside the `(list, tuple)` arm — the split the previous arm deferred. Without it `(1, 2)` and `[1, 2]` render identically and collide in `repr_hash`, and the `len(obj) == 1` sub-branch exists to reproduce Python's own trailing-comma repr so `(1,)` does not render as the parenthesised expression `(1)`. This is the one place in this module where tuple-ness is semantic rather than incidental. Invalidated if tuples are normalized to lists before reaching `repr_hash`, as they are on the `canonical_json` path.

R5 `isinstance(obj, (list, tuple))` in `_stable_repr`. Grouped because both need the same element-wise recursive join; unlike the `canonical_json` path at line 59, this arm does NOT collapse tuple into list — it defers the distinction to line 118, because repr fidelity is the product here rather than a canonical hash input. Ordering matters against the set arm above: list and tuple are not sets, so the arms are disjoint and their relative order is free, but this arm must stay below the dict arm so that no Mapping reaches it. Invalidated if a new ordered container type must hash like a list.
contracts/hashing.py:R5:is_lower_sha256_: R5 `isinstance(value, str)` as the first conjunct of `is_lower_sha256_hex`, a function whose declared return type is `TypeGuard[str]`. The isinstance is not a defensive afterthought here: it IS the evidence the TypeGuard exports to callers, and the parameter is typed `object` precisely so callers may hand it an unverified digest field read back out of the audit store. It is also load-bearing at runtime — `re.fullmatch` raises TypeError on a non-str/bytes argument, so without the guard a None or int digest crashes instead of answering False. A duck-typed probe would be wrong in the other direction: `bytes` satisfies `re.fullmatch` against this ASCII pattern, and a bytes digest must NOT be accepted as a lowercase hex string. Invalidated if `value` is narrowed to `str` in the signature (the check then becomes dead and should be deleted, not sealed) or if the return type stops being a TypeGuard.
core/canonical.py:R5:_normalize_for_cano: R5 `isinstance(data, PipelineRow)` — the one site in this module that narrows against a concrete class ELSPETH itself defines, which is exactly the nominal-typing half of ADR-032 ("nominally type what ELSPETH owns"). PipelineRow is NOT a Mapping and NOT a dict (verified), so its position above the Mapping arm is not an ordering constraint; the arm is needed because without it a PipelineRow matches no arm at all, falls through to `_normalize_value`, and returns unchanged into rfc8785. The body calls `to_dict()` so everything downstream sees a plain Mapping and the row's field values get normalized individually. Invalidated if PipelineRow registers as a Mapping (the arm would then be reachable-but-redundant and should be deleted), or if `to_dict()` stops returning the audit-relevant field set.

R5 `isinstance(data, Mapping)` against the ABC, not `dict` — same MappingProxyType reasoning as `contracts/hashing.py:57`, but this arm carries an extra responsibility: it detects a user mapping that already contains the reserved `__elspeth_canonical_type__` key and re-encodes it as an explicit sorted `entries` list. Without that branch, user data could forge a canonical type tag and change how the hash reader interprets the record. Note the deliberate contrast with `sanitize_for_canonical` at line 309, which tests `dict`: this arm serves the Tier-1 owned-data path where deep_freeze proxies genuinely appear. Invalidated if the reserved key is renamed without the reader changing, or if deep_freeze stops producing MappingProxyType.

R5 `isinstance(data, list | tuple)` — recursion into sequences, collapsing tuple to list because the output is a hash input and tuple-ness is not semantic on this path (the checkpoint serializer makes the opposite call for the same types, correctly, because it needs round-trip fidelity). Placed after the Mapping arm so that a Mapping is never treated as an iterable of its keys, which is what would happen if a generic-iterable test were used instead of these two named types. Invalidated the moment a caller needs `(1, 2)` and `[1, 2]` to produce different digests.
core/canonical.py:R5:_normalize_value:as: R5 `isinstance(obj, datetime)` — the stdlib arm, and it is fenced on BOTH sides by ordering constraints. Above it: pd.Timestamp (line 117) and the pd.NA/pd.NaT sentinel arm (line 124), both of which are datetime subclasses or instances and would be wrongly captured here if they came later — pd.NaT in particular would be rendered as a real timestamp instead of the intended missing value. Below it: `date` at line 133, which is datetime's SUPERCLASS, so swapping those two would silently truncate every timestamp in the audit trail to a bare date. Naive datetimes are assumed UTC by explicit documented policy rather than rejected. Invalidated by any reordering of the arms between lines 117 and 133.

R5 `isinstance(obj, date)` — reachable only by true dates, because datetime (its subclass) is consumed at line 128. The arm is separate from the datetime arm rather than merged because a date has no timezone to normalize and no time component to render: `date.isoformat()` produces "YYYY-MM-DD", and forcing a date through the datetime path would fabricate a midnight UTC instant the source never asserted. That fabrication is the integrity risk this split avoids. Invalidated if the audit contract requires dates and datetimes to share one representation.

R5 `isinstance(obj, time)` — a wall-clock time with no date, kept as its own arm because it is unrelated to the date/datetime hierarchy above (time is not a date subclass) and would otherwise fall through to `return obj` and reach rfc8785 unserializable. Rendered with `isoformat()`, which preserves any tzinfo the value carries; unlike the datetime arm this one does NOT impose UTC, because a naive time has no instant to localize against and inventing one would be fabrication. Invalidated if naive times acquire a documented timezone policy the way naive datetimes have one.

R5 `isinstance(obj, UUID)` — UUID is not a str and not JSON-native, so without this arm it reaches rfc8785 unserializable. `str(obj)` yields the canonical hyphenated lowercase form, which is what makes the digest stable across UUIDs constructed from bytes, ints, or a differently-cased string: three inputs that are equal as UUIDs must hash equal. That normalization, not the type dispatch, is the audit-integrity content of this arm. Invalidated if UUIDs must round-trip as a distinct type rather than as a string — the checkpoint serializer, which does need round-trip fidelity, tags them with an envelope instead.

R5 `isinstance(obj, bytes)` — the one arm in this function that emits a TAGGED structure (`{__elspeth_canonical_type__: "bytes", base64: ...}`) rather than a bare primitive. The tag is required for collision safety: a bare base64 string would hash identically to a genuine string field whose content happens to be that base64 text, silently merging two distinct audit values. JSON has no byte type, so some encoding is unavoidable; making it self-describing is what keeps it injective. Invalidated if a bytes encoding is chosen that cannot collide with string data, or if the reserved type key changes without the reader changing with it.

R5 `isinstance(obj, Decimal)` — the last named arm, and the only one whose finiteness check uses `obj.is_finite()`. That method rejects four states Python floats cannot even represent as distinct values: NaN, sNaN, +Infinity and -Infinity. The body then emits `str(obj)`, NOT `float(obj)`, and that is the point of the arm: Decimal exists precisely because the value cannot be represented exactly as a binary float, so converting it for hashing would make the digest disagree with the value the audit trail claims to record. Invalidated if the audit contract stops accepting Decimal on `object`-typed fields, or if a JSON encoding for exact decimals is adopted.

R5 `isinstance(obj, np.floating)` — first arm of `_normalize_value`, and both its position and its abstract base are load-bearing. `np.floating` covers float16/32/64/longdouble; of those only np.float64 subclasses Python `float`, so without this arm np.float32 and np.longdouble would miss the `float` arm at line 79 AND every arm below it, falling through to the trailing `return obj` and reaching rfc8785 as an unserializable object. For np.float64 the arm must also come FIRST, ahead of the float arm, so that finiteness is tested with numpy-native `np.isfinite` rather than `math.isnan`/`isinf` — the latter narrow through `float()`, which overflows for np.longdouble values outside IEEE-754 double range and would falsely reject a finite value as infinite. The second, post-conversion `math.isfinite` check in the body is the deliberate complement: a value finite as longdouble can genuinely overflow when narrowed for JSON, and that case gets its own distinct error message. Invalidated if numpy scalar types stop subclassing float, or if the two arms are reordered.

R5 `isinstance(obj, float)` — the plain-Python-float arm, reachable only after np.floating has been consumed above. That is why it may safely use `math.isnan`/`math.isinf`: a true Python float is by construction inside IEEE-754 double range, so the downcast-overflow hazard that forces numpy-native checks one arm up does not exist here. NaN/Infinity rejection is Tier-1 audit integrity — the crash path is a ValueError out of `canonical_json`/`stable_hash` into the audit write, which is preferred over emitting a digest over a value that JSON cannot represent. Invalidated if a non-numpy float subclass with extended range is introduced, which would need the same treatment as np.longdouble.

R5 `isinstance(obj, str | int | bool)` in `obj is None or isinstance(...)` — the JSON-native passthrough. `bool` is named explicitly even though bool is a subclass of int, because the intent (booleans stay booleans and are never coerced to 0/1) must survive a future reordering or a narrowing of the union. The arm's POSITION is the integrity-relevant fact: it sits below both float arms, so a NaN can never reach passthrough and escape the finiteness gate. PEP 604 union syntax rather than a tuple is house style in this module. Invalidated if any of these primitives acquires a normalization requirement — e.g. int range clamping for consumers that cannot carry values beyond 2**53.

R5 `isinstance(obj, np.integer)` — necessary because np.int64 is NOT a subclass of Python int (verified, unlike np.float64 which does subclass float). Without this arm every numpy integer falls through to `return obj` and reaches rfc8785 unserializable. No finiteness question arises for integers, so unlike the np.floating arm the conversion is total and needs no guard. Invalidated if numpy integers must carry values outside the range JSON consumers can represent exactly — np.uint64 above 2**53 already loses precision in JavaScript readers, and closing that would mean adding a range check here, not removing the arm.

R5 `isinstance(obj, np.bool_)` — its own arm because np.bool_ subclasses neither `bool` nor `int` (verified), so it is caught by no other test in this function and would otherwise reach rfc8785 as an unserializable object. It cannot be folded into the np.integer arm above for the same reason: converting it with `int()` would silently turn an audit-recorded True into 1 and change the JSON type of the field. Invalidated if numpy makes np.bool_ a bool subclass, at which point the primitive passthrough at line 85 would cover it.

R5 `isinstance(obj, np.ndarray)` — a container arm among scalar arms, and the only one whose body performs a vectorised integrity check: `np.all(np.isfinite(obj))` over numeric dtypes, which is what makes NaN rejection affordable for large arrays instead of per-element recursion. Object and string dtypes deliberately skip the vector check and are normalized element-by-element below so embedded Python floats still hit the scalar guards. `isinstance` rather than an exact type check so ndarray subclasses (np.matrix, masked arrays) take the same path rather than falling through unserialized. Invalidated if masked arrays need distinct missing-value semantics — today their fill values are normalized like any other element, which is a real limitation this arm papers over.

R5 `isinstance(obj, np.datetime64)` — required because np.datetime64 is NOT a datetime subclass (verified), so the stdlib `datetime` arm at line 128 cannot see it. The body does two things nothing else does: `np.isnat` maps numpy's own not-a-time sentinel to None (parallel to the pd.NA/pd.NaT arm), and conversion through pd.Timestamp yields the single UTC ISO-8601 output format shared with the pandas arm, so a timestamp hashes identically regardless of which library produced it. That shared output format is the audit-integrity property here. Invalidated if the canonical timestamp representation stops being UTC ISO-8601, or if np.datetime64 gains sub-nanosecond units pd.Timestamp cannot carry.

R5 `isinstance(obj, pd.Timestamp)` — and this arm's POSITION above the stdlib `datetime` arm at line 128 is strictly load-bearing, because pd.Timestamp IS a datetime subclass (verified). If the arms were swapped, every pandas timestamp would be normalized by the stdlib path — localized with `replace(tzinfo=UTC)` instead of pandas' own `tz_localize`, and rendered by datetime.isoformat rather than Timestamp.isoformat, which is where nanosecond precision lives. Keeping pandas values inside pandas' own timezone API is the reason the arm exists at all. Invalidated if pd.Timestamp stops subclassing datetime, or if nanosecond precision stops being part of the audit contract.
core/canonical.py:R5:sanitize_for_canoni: R5 `isinstance(obj, dict)` opening `sanitize_for_canonical` — the Tier-3 quarantine path, where non-finite floats are REPLACED with None rather than rejected, because the data is already known bad and the quarantine record must still be hashable. Worth stating plainly: this arm tests `dict` while the Tier-1 sibling `_normalize_for_canonical` at line 175 tests `Mapping`. That asymmetry is deliberate and currently correct — quarantined rows arrive from source readers as plain dicts, not as deep_freeze proxies — but it is the arm's real limitation: a MappingProxyType reaching here would fall through to `return obj` unsanitized. Invalidated the moment a frozen or proxy mapping can reach the quarantine path, at which point this must widen to Mapping.

R5 `isinstance(obj, np.ndarray)` in the quarantine path. Placed ABOVE the `(list, tuple)` arm and converted with `.tolist()` first, which matters because an ndarray is not a list and would otherwise reach the float arms as a whole array — where `math.isnan(array)` raises TypeError rather than answering, turning a quarantine into a crash. Unlike the Tier-1 arm at line 93 this one does no vectorised finiteness check: it does not need to detect non-finite values, only to replace them, so element-wise recursion after tolist() is sufficient and simpler. Invalidated if quarantine sanitization becomes performance-bound on large arrays, which would call for a vectorised `np.nan_to_num`-style path.

R5 `isinstance(obj, (list, tuple))` in the quarantine path — recursion into sequences, returning a list in both cases. Tuple collapse is acceptable here for the same reason as line 189 (the output feeds a hash, not a round-trip) and is additionally harmless because quarantined data is not restored to a typed contract. Positioned below the ndarray arm so arrays are converted before being treated as sequences. Invalidated if sanitized output is ever fed back into a typed contract that distinguishes tuple from list.

R5 `isinstance(obj, float)` in `isinstance(obj, float) and (math.isnan(obj) or math.isinf(obj))` — the quarantine counterpart of the Tier-1 rejection at line 79, and the inversion of policy is the point: here a non-finite float becomes None instead of raising, because the caller has already recorded WHY the data was quarantined and the audit value of the record is preserved by the surrounding error message. The isinstance conjunct is required, not decorative: math.isnan raises TypeError on a str or None, so dropping it would crash on exactly the malformed input this function exists to absorb. Invalidated if quarantine adopts a non-None sentinel for non-finite values, or if the surrounding error message stops recording the original defect.

R5 `isinstance(obj, np.floating)` in `isinstance(obj, np.floating) and not np.isfinite(obj)` — a SECOND float arm below the plain-float one at 315, and it is not redundant with it: np.float32 and np.longdouble do not subclass Python float (verified), so line 315 cannot see them at all. `np.isfinite` rather than `math.isfinite(float(obj))` for the same longdouble-overflow reason documented on the Tier-1 arm at line 66 — the narrowing cast would report a finite longdouble as infinite and null out a value that was fine. Unlike the Tier-1 arm this one has no post-conversion guard, because the quarantine path returns the numpy scalar unchanged when it is finite rather than narrowing it. Invalidated if quarantined numpy scalars must be narrowed to Python floats before hashing, which would reintroduce the overflow case.
core/checkpoint/serialization.py:R5:Chec: R5 `isinstance(obj, datetime)` — first arm of `CheckpointEncoder.default`, and the code comment above it states the invariant this arm enforces: datetime MUST be tested before `date` at line 136 because datetime subclasses date. Swapping them would tag every timestamp as a "date" envelope, and `checkpoint_loads` would then restore a `date` where the aggregation state held a datetime — silent type corruption on the resume path, not a crash. The body also normalizes naive datetimes to UTC before rendering, so a checkpoint written in one process timezone restores identically in another. Invalidated by any reordering of the arms in this method, which is why the ordering is documented in-line rather than left implicit.

R5 `isinstance(obj, Decimal)` — the arm carries a finiteness guard that exists specifically because the write-side pre-pass cannot: `_reject_nan_infinity` inspects only Python `float`, so `Decimal("NaN")` would pass that walk untouched, serialize as the string "NaN" inside a decimal envelope, and be restored by `checkpoint_loads` as a live non-finite Decimal in the Tier-1 audit trail. This arm is the write half of a matched pair with the `is_finite()` re-check in `_restore_types`; the symmetry is deliberate and documented at both ends. `str(obj)` rather than float() preserves the exact value, as on the canonical-hashing path. Invalidated if `_reject_nan_infinity` is widened to cover Decimal, which would make this the second of two guards rather than the only one.

R5 `isinstance(obj, date)` — reachable only after the datetime arm at line 116 has consumed datetime instances, which is the ordering constraint documented there. The arm is separate rather than merged because the envelope TAG differs ("date" vs "datetime") and the tags drive `_restore_types`: merging them would force the reader to guess from the string shape whether a time component was present, which is exactly the shape-sniffing this module's envelope design replaced. Invalidated if the two tags are unified, which would require the restore side to distinguish them another way.

R5 `isinstance(obj, time)` — a wall-clock time is not a date and not a datetime, so it is caught by neither arm above and would otherwise fall to this method's terminal TypeError and abort a checkpoint write on a legitimate value. `time` reaches here through SchemaContract's `object`-typed fields and FLEXIBLE/OBSERVED-mode rows, which is why the module supports it at all. Its `isoformat()` round-trips exactly through `time.fromisoformat` on the restore side, so the envelope is lossless. Invalidated if `time` is removed from the set of types a row payload may carry.

R5 `isinstance(obj, bytes)` — base64 into a tagged envelope. The tag is what makes the encoding injective: without it, restored data could not distinguish a bytes field from a string field whose content is that same base64 text. The restore side is stricter than a plain decode — it validates canonical base64 and re-encodes to confirm round-trip equality — so a tampered or non-canonically-encoded payload is rejected rather than silently decoded to different bytes. This arm is the write half of that pair. Invalidated if the bytes encoding changes without `_restore_bytes_envelope` changing with it.

R5 `isinstance(obj, UUID)` — envelope-tagged rather than emitted as a bare string, which is the deliberate difference from `core/canonical.py:139` where a UUID becomes a plain string. The divergence is the module's whole reason for existing: canonical.py produces a hash input where type is not recoverable and does not need to be, while this serializer must restore a UUID as a UUID so that aggregation state resumes with the same types it was suspended with. Invalidated if checkpoint payloads stop requiring round-trip type fidelity.

R5 `isinstance(obj, np.floating)` — and note this arm deliberately does NOT emit an envelope: it returns a plain Python float, because numpy-ness carries no semantic meaning for the audit trail while the VALUE does. That policy choice (documented in the module header) is what distinguishes it from every arm above it. The two-stage finiteness check is the same longdouble reasoning as `core/canonical.py:66`: `np.isfinite` first because `math.isnan` would narrow through `float()` and overflow, then `math.isfinite` on the narrowed result because a value genuinely finite as longdouble can overflow when converted for JSON — and the second failure gets its own message so the two causes are distinguishable in an incident. Invalidated if numpy scalars must round-trip as numpy scalars, which would make this an envelope arm.

R5 `isinstance(obj, np.integer)` — needed because np.int64 does not subclass Python int (verified), so json's native encoder never sees it as a number and it would reach this method's terminal TypeError. Converted with `int()` and NOT tagged, following the same numpy-ness-is-not-semantic policy as the np.floating arm above. Unlike that arm it needs no finiteness guard, because integers have no non-finite states. Invalidated if numpy integers must carry values outside the range JSON consumers can represent exactly, which would need a range check here rather than removal of the arm.

R5 `isinstance(obj, np.bool_)` — its own arm because np.bool_ subclasses neither bool nor int (verified), so neither the np.integer arm above nor json's native bool handling can see it, and it would otherwise reach the terminal TypeError. It cannot be folded into the np.integer arm: `int()` would restore a recorded True as the number 1, changing the JSON type of an audit field. This is the smallest arm in the method and the one most likely to look redundant to a reader who assumes numpy booleans behave like Python ones. Invalidated if numpy makes np.bool_ a bool subclass.
core/checkpoint/serialization.py:R5:_esc: R5 `isinstance(obj, datetime)` in `_escape_reserved_keys` — an explicit passthrough arm, and it must be judged honestly: a datetime matches none of the dict/tuple/list arms below it, so today this branch is behaviourally equivalent to the function's trailing `return obj`. It is retained deliberately rather than deleted because it encodes a real invariant that the trailing return only satisfies by accident — "datetimes belong to CheckpointEncoder and must NOT be rewritten during pre-processing" — and this function is the pre-pass where a future arm (a `date` arm, say, since datetime subclasses date) would otherwise silently capture them and produce a wrong envelope. Unlike a redundant term inside a boolean expression, this branch's redundancy is a global property of the current arm set, not a local logical identity, which is why it is justified rather than removed. Invalidated the moment an arm is added below it that could match a datetime — at which point this stops being a no-op and starts doing its job — or if the invariant is instead enforced by a test over the arm set, which would make the branch genuinely deletable.

R5 `isinstance(obj, tuple)` in `_escape_reserved_keys` — the one arm in this module that MUST run during pre-processing rather than in the encoder, and the in-line comment says why: json.dumps turns a tuple into a JSON array and never calls `default()`, so `CheckpointEncoder` gets no chance to tag it. Without this arm a tuple silently restores as a list and aggregation state resumes with a different type than it was suspended with. The arm recurses into elements while building the envelope so nested tuples are tagged too. Invalidated if json.dumps gains a hook for tuple, or if tuple/list equivalence becomes acceptable in checkpoint payloads.

R5 `isinstance(obj, dict)` in `_escape_reserved_keys` — the collision-safety arm. It recurses FIRST and only then tests whether the resulting dict contains a reserved envelope key, which is the correct order: a nested user dict carrying the reserved key must be escaped at its own level before the parent decides about itself. This is the mechanism that lets user data legitimately contain `__elspeth_type__` without being mistaken for a type envelope on restore — the security property the module header describes as replacing the old shape-based tags. `dict` rather than Mapping matches what json.dumps will actually serialize. Invalidated if the reserved key names change without `_restore_types` changing, or if the recurse-then-test order is swapped.

R5 `isinstance(obj, list)` in `_escape_reserved_keys` — recursion into lists so that dicts nested inside arrays are escaped too. Deliberately `list` alone and not `(list, tuple)`, because tuple was already consumed by the envelope arm at line 244 and must NOT be re-flattened into a list here; grouping them, as several sibling functions in this codebase do, would silently undo the tuple envelope that arm just built. That asymmetry with the surrounding modules is the reason this arm looks wrong at a glance and is right in fact. Invalidated if the tuple arm is removed or moved below this one.

R5 `isinstance(node.func.value, ast.Name)` in `visit_Call` — pins the `.get` receiver to a bare name before it is matched against `_allowed_names`. Without it, an expression of the form `(anything).get('x')` would enter the permissive branch and have its arguments validated as though it were a row read, instead of falling through to "Forbidden function call". This is the conjunct that keeps the call whitelist rooted rather than shape-based. Invalidated if receivers other than bare allowed names become callable.

R5 `isinstance(node.func, ast.Name)` — the safe-builtin call branch, and the ONLY route by which a callable other than `.get` is admitted. Paired with `node.func.id in _SAFE_BUILTINS`, it enforces that builtins may be called only in direct `name(...)` form; the module header explains why that matters — the four str callables are unbound `str.*` descriptors, so a direct call raises a TypeError that `visit_Call` wraps cleanly, while an indirect reference would leak a raw AttributeError through `evaluate()`'s crash-through tuple. Invalidated if callables are admitted in any form other than a bare name, or if `_SAFE_BUILTINS` gains an entry that is not a descriptor.

R5 `isinstance(op, ast.Is | ast.IsNot)` in `visit_Compare`, reached only in the `elif` after the operator has been confirmed to be in `_COMPARISON_OPS`. It selects the two operators that get an EXTRA restriction the others do not: identity comparison is permitted only against None. That restriction exists because `is` over row data compares object identity, which for interned or boxed values is an implementation detail and would make a gate's routing depend on CPython's caching rather than on the data. Note the deliberate mix of styles in this method — `type(op) not in _COMPARISON_OPS` for exact membership above, `isinstance` here where subclass matching is wanted. Invalidated if identity comparison is permitted against further sentinels, or forbidden outright.

R5 `isinstance(node.value, float)` in `visit_Constant`, guarding `math.isfinite`. This is parse-time rejection of a non-finite float LITERAL — a config author writing `inf` or `nan` into a gate condition — which must be caught here rather than at evaluation because the parser's contract is that a constructed ExpressionParser is safe to evaluate. The isinstance is required, not decorative: `math.isfinite` raises TypeError on a str or None constant, both of which reach this method routinely. Placed before the general primitive arm at 358 so a non-finite float is rejected rather than admitted as an allowed float. Invalidated if non-finite literals become meaningful in gate conditions, or if the evaluator's own `_ensure_finite_float` is judged sufficient (it is not — it runs too late to keep the construction-time contract).

R5 `isinstance(node.value, str | int | float | bool)` — the constant whitelist, and it is a whitelist rather than a blacklist by design: anything not named here falls to the explicit "Forbidden constant type" error. That fail-closed polarity is what stops exotic literal types (bytes, complex, Ellipsis) from entering the sandbox merely because no rule mentions them. Reached only after the None arm and the non-finite float arm above have run, so by this point a float constant is known finite. Invalidated if a new literal type is admitted to the grammar, which must be an addition HERE and not a loosening elsewhere.

R5 `isinstance(node.slice, ast.Slice)` in `visit_Subscript` — defense-in-depth, and knowingly duplicated: `visit_Slice` rejects slice syntax on its own, and this check rejects it again at the subscript level. The duplication is deliberate because the two guards fail independently — a future change to visitor dispatch could stop `visit_Slice` from being reached for a slice nested in a subscript, and this arm would still hold. Slices are forbidden because `row['a':'b']` has no meaning over row data and the grammar admits subscripts only for field access. Invalidated if slice support is added, which would require removing both guards together.
